newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Desperate Russia nuclear scientist commits suicide.
newsitem.headline: Desperate Russia nuclear scientist commits suicide.

text.p: A top Russian nuclear physicist has committed suicide after apparently losing hope of keeping afloat the once top-secret research centre he headed, his deputy said on Thursday.
Vladimir Nechai, 60, shot himself on Wednesday in his office Russia's second largest nuclear research centre in the Urals town of Snezhinsk more than 1,000 km (600 miles) east of Moscow.
Vladislav Nikitin, deputy head of the Federal Nuclear Centre which was formerly known as Chelyabinsk-70, said Nechai had left a letter on his table which had been taken away by police investigators.
"All we know is that his decision was prompted by constant stress," Nikitin told Reuters by telephone from Snezhinsk.
He said he could not say exactly what provoked the suicide but that Nechai's stress had been brought on as he fought for the survival of his centre, where workers had not been paid since May.
As at many other nuclear centres in Russia, problems have mounted because the government has all but stopped funding scientific research in hard economic times.
Nikitin said Nechai, a theoretician who worked almost 40 years on Soviet and Russian nuclear programmes, and his associates had tried hard to ensure the survival of his centre.

"We have sent letters to the president (Boris Yeltsin), to parliament, to (Prime Minister Viktor) Chernomyrdin, but there has been no reply," he said. "The situation has not improved, and I don't see any prospect of it improving."
"All these problems have been accumulating for months. But of course, no one would say now what exactly was on his mind when made this fatal decision."
Nikitin said employees at Chelyabinsk-70 had not been paid since May and many families were close to starvation.
"We are now in a battle with trade unions over the wage delays although everyone understands this was not the director's fault," he said.
Nikitin said nuclear centres, kept in isolation from the outside world for decades, had even more headaches to deal with than other struggling and underfunded scientific institutions.

"We live in a so-called 'closed administrative territory' and there are no other jobs than in the centre," he said. "If we start sacking people, which we are forced to do, this will be a catastrophe not only for the centre, but for the whole town."
Nikitin said the Arzamas-16 centre, the only nuclear research centre in Russia bigger than the one at Snezhinsk, and other smaller institutions faced similar problems.

Yuri Osipov, who was elected head of the influential Academy of Sciences this week, said in a television interview on Wednesday that many top Russian scientists were paid the equivalent of only about $200 a month.

Senior scientists in many areas, from computers to aviation and defence technology, have been forced to supplement their income by taking up secondary occupations such as taxi driving or gardening. Many have had to leave their profession altogether. Osipov said Russia faced a "brain drain" and made clear there were fears that some scientists could be lured to go to countries which are trying to build nuclear arms.
